title: Year five opens: the sources themselves
hook: four years of learning about the texts; this year, reading them, then living them
tomorrow: year one stopped at Avot chapter two. what's in the rest?

segments.voice: Year four closed on Hillel's two easy-to-skip words: go and learn. The line was Judaism thinks and lives. Today, the going starts.

There's a ten-minute video for plenty of books: the plot, the themes, the twist, explained by someone who did the reading. You can know about a book for years and never open it. For four years, this path has done a lot of that for you: who said what, what the rabbis argued, how the prayers are built. A good map. But a map isn't the walk. So, one question for the year: why read the old texts yourself, and what happens once you have?
screen: `TEN MINUTES, NO BOOK.` → `A MAP ISN'T THE WALK.` → `WHY READ IT YOURSELF?`

segments.voice: The sages asked nearly the same question, out loud, gathered in an upper room in the town of Lod. The Talmud tells it. Which is greater, study or deed? Rabbi Tarfon answered: deed. Rabbi Akiva answered: study. Then the whole room answered together: study is greater, because study leads to deed. Read that twice. They don't pick reading over living. They put reading first because it's the road to living. That's this year, in order: the sources themselves, the rest of Pirkei Avot saying by saying, a tractate of Talmud, Maimonides on returning, the midrash; then a long stretch on living it. The Torah's own book of songs gives the reading a rhythm. The first psalm, in the JPS 1917 translation: "But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in His law doth he meditate day and night." Not once. Day and night: a habit with a place in the day. Here's ground Jews share with Christian neighbors. That same psalm sits in Christian Bibles too. And in the book of Acts, the people of Berea are praised because they, in the King James words, "searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so." Every day, and checking for yourself. One honest difference: in Christian Bibles those scriptures sit beside the New Testament and are read in the light of Jesus. Jews read them beside the oral Torah: the Mishnah, the Talmud, the voices of Avot, argued in pairs. The same psalm, with different companions at the table.
screen: `STUDY OR DEED? THE ROOM IN LOD.` · `STUDY, BECAUSE IT LEADS TO DEED.` · `DAY AND NIGHT: PSALM 1.` · `SEARCHED THE SCRIPTURES DAILY.` · then, large: `READ, THEN LIVE.`

segments.voice: Choose the spot where this year's reading will happen: one chair, a corner of the kitchen table, the same seat on the bus. If you can, go and sit there now; if not, see it clearly, the light, the sounds, where the book or the phone will rest. Stay there for the sit, and let it become the place you come back to.
Year five opens. The last year of the path: the sources themselves, read closely, and then the life they lead to.
Hold on to this: read, then live, because study is headed somewhere. Year five, underway.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition speaks of fixing a set time for Torah study; some learn alone, some with a study partner (chavruta), some a daily page of Talmud, and Psalm 1's 'day and night' is often read as that steady habit.

chat.says: saba's moving to a small apartment and says take any books i want. why keep ones i'll never read?
options: Keep a few you'll actually open. Study comes first because it leads to living.

chat.meaning: In the Talmud the sages say study is greater because it leads to deed. Books you open are the road; read, then live.

Talmud.meaning: the rabbis' great record of discussion on the Mishnah

Lod.meaning: a town in the land of Israel where the sages met

Akiva.meaning: a sage of the Mishnah, who answered: study

Pirkei Avot.meaning: chapters of the fathers: the sages' sayings

Berea.meaning: a town in the book of Acts whose people searched the scriptures

Mishnah.meaning: the oral Torah, set down in writing
